sousTitre: The complete history of artificial intelligence, from the first machines to today's agents

diapos.sousTitre: The complete history of artificial intelligence, from the first machines to today's agents
diapos.notes: Welcome the class with a question on the board: “Can a machine think?” Do not answer it: the whole lesson keeps coming back to it. Announce the common thread: the dream of intelligent machines is very old, but AI as a science is seventy years old, and its agents only a few years.

points: The dream of machines (from Antiquity to 1945)
The birth of AI (1950–1956)
The golden age, then the first winter (1956–1980)
Expert systems (1980–1993)
Learning from data (1990–2016)
The deep learning revolution (2006–2016)
Transformers and generative AI (2017–2022)
The age of agents (2023–2026)
diapos.notes: Eight stages, each with a key date to remember. Suggest that students write down one date per stage: they will rebuild the timeline at the end.

diapos.titre: And you, what do you call “intelligence”?
points: Understanding a sentence, translating a poem
Recognizing one face among a thousand
Winning at chess, solving a problem
Learning from one's mistakes
Acting alone to reach a goal
diapos.notes: Two minutes of voting by show of hands: which of these abilities does a machine already have? The answer at the end of the lesson: all of them, to varying degrees, but no machine combines them as a human does. The last line, acting alone to reach a goal, defines the agent: it is where the lesson is heading.

diapos.texte: Long before computers, humans imagined and built machines that imitate life, then machines that calculate.
diapos.notes: First stage: AI did not come from nowhere. Two lines meet here: automata, which imitate movement, and calculating machines, which imitate reasoning.

points: Greek myth: Talos, a bronze giant who guards Crete
1st century: Hero of Alexandria describes theater automata
1739: Vaucanson's duck flaps its wings and “digests”
Around 1770: the Jaquet-Droz Writer traces letters with a quill
diapos.notes: An automaton reproduces a movement set in advance by its gears or cams. It decides nothing: that is the difference from an AI. Ask: does the Jaquet-Droz Writer really “write”?

diapos.titre: Al-Jazari, the engineer of ingenious machines
points: Engineer at the Artuqid court, in Upper Mesopotamia
In 1206, writes *The Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices*
Describes some fifty machines: clocks, pumps, automata
His elephant clock marks the hours with automata
diapos.notes: Al-Jazari shows that the tradition of automata runs through the medieval Arab and Muslim world. His detailed drawings still make it possible to rebuild his machines today. Be careful: these are automata programmed in advance, not machines that learn.

points: 1642: Blaise Pascal builds the Pascaline, which adds
1673: Leibniz presents a machine that multiplies
1837: Charles Babbage designs the Analytical Engine, programmable with punched cards
The Analytical Engine would never be completed in his lifetime
diapos.notes: A key transition: a machine that calculates takes over part of the work of the mind. Babbage's Analytical Engine already has a memory and a calculating unit, like our computers.

points: 1843: her notes on Babbage's Analytical Engine
In them, she writes an algorithm to compute Bernoulli numbers
She imagines that the machine could compose music
diapos.citation: The Analytical Engine has no pretensions whatever to originate anything.
diapos.notes: Her sentence, “Lady Lovelace's objection”, would be discussed by Turing a century later: does a machine only do what it is told? A question for the class: does a model that writes a poem create something?

points: 1854: George Boole reduces reasoning to calculations on true and false
1936: Alan Turing describes an abstract machine capable of any calculation
A tape, a read head, a table of rules: the “Turing machine”
Every computer today is, in principle, a Turing machine
diapos.notes: Boole provides the alphabet (true, false, and, or, not); Turing provides the universal machine. Show the animation: the head reads a cell, writes, moves, changes state. With rules this simple, anything can be calculated.

diapos.role: Mathematician, father of theoretical computer science
points: 1936: the universal machine
1939–1945: helps break the Enigma code at Bletchley Park
1950: “Computing Machinery and Intelligence”, the founding paper
diapos.citation: I propose to consider the question, ‘Can machines think?’
diapos.notes: Turing replaces an impossible question (“think”) with an observable test, the imitation game. This is the founding move of AI. The quoted sentence opens his 1950 paper.

points: Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts model a neuron as a calculation
It adds up input signals and “fires” above a threshold
It is the ancestor of all today's neural networks
diapos.notes: The first bridge between biology and calculation. Draw on the board: three inputs, weights, a sum, a threshold. We will find exactly this diagram again with the perceptron in 1958, then in deep learning.

points: 1945: ENIAC, 30 tonnes, calculates ballistic trajectories
1948: Claude Shannon founds information theory
The bit becomes the unit of all information: text, image, sound
The machines finally exist; now they must be made “intelligent”
diapos.notes: ENIAC fills an entire room and is programmed by plugging in cables. Shannon, for his part, would be one of the four signatories of the Dartmouth proposal. End of the first stage: everything is ready for the birth of AI.

diapos.texte: In six years, a question becomes a research program, then a discipline with a name.
diapos.notes: Second stage: three moments to remember: 1950 (Turing), 1956 (Dartmouth) and the first “intelligent” program.

points: A judge converses in writing with two hidden interlocutors
One is a human, the other a machine
If the judge cannot tell them apart, the machine “passes”
diapos.notes: Act out the scene: two hidden volunteers, a judge, five minutes of written questions. Discussion: does the test measure intelligence, or the art of creating an illusion? Today's chatbots have revived this debate.

diapos.texte: Every aspect of learning or any other feature of intelligence can in principle be so precisely described that a machine can be made to simulate it.
diapos.auteur: J. McCarthy, M. Minsky, N. Rochester, C. Shannon
diapos.source: Proposal for the Dartmouth workshop, August 31, 1955
diapos.notes: This is the text in which the expression “artificial intelligence” appears. The hypothesis is very ambitious: everything intelligence does could be described precisely. Ask: is that true of humor? Of poetic intuition?

diapos.role: Computer scientist who gave AI its name
points: Summer 1956: organizes the Dartmouth workshop, the birth certificate of AI
1958: creates the Lisp language, long the language of AI
With him: Marvin Minsky, Claude Shannon, Nathaniel Rochester
diapos.notes: The Dartmouth workshop brought together about ten researchers during the summer of 1956. It produced no major discovery, but it gave the discipline a name, a community and a program.

points: The Logic Theorist by Allen Newell, Herbert Simon and Cliff Shaw
It proves 38 of the first 52 theorems of *Principia Mathematica*
For one of them, a more elegant proof than the authors' own
A key idea: searching among possibilities with rules
diapos.notes: The Logic Theorist embodies symbolic AI: symbols, rules, a search through a tree of possibilities. It is the same logic as forward chaining in the chapter 3 tutorial (TD).

diapos.titre: The golden age, then the first winter
diapos.texte: Spectacular successes, excessive promises, then disappointment and the end of funding.
diapos.notes: Third stage: this is the first cycle of enthusiasm and disillusion. It will repeat itself, which helps us judge today's promises.

points: Frank Rosenblatt builds a machine that learns to recognize shapes
It adjusts its own weights after each error
The press announces machines that “think”: enthusiasm runs wild
diapos.notes: The perceptron is the first neural network that learns. Link it to the “human neuron” activity in the guide: weights, a threshold, a correction after each error.

points: Arthur Samuel writes a checkers program that improves by playing
He coins the term “machine learning”
The program ends up beating its own creator
Two paths emerge: writing the rules, or having them learned
diapos.notes: Here is the opposition that structures the whole history: symbolic AI (we write the rules) versus connectionist or statistical AI (the machine learns them from examples).

echanges.texte: They're always bugging us about something or other.
CAN YOU THINK OF A SPECIFIC EXAMPLE
Well, my boyfriend made me come here.
YOUR BOYFRIEND MADE YOU COME HERE

diapos.notes: ELIZA understands nothing: it spots keywords and sends the sentence back using transformation rules. Yet users confided their secrets to it. Weizenbaum was troubled by this all his life. This is the “ELIZA effect”: attributing understanding to a machine that answers well.

diapos.titre: Shakey, the first robot that reasons
points: Built at the Stanford Research Institute (SRI)
It perceives its environment with a camera
It plans a sequence of actions to reach a goal
The A* algorithm, still used to compute routes, was created for it
diapos.notes: Shakey is a direct ancestor of agents: it perceives, plans, acts. But it takes minutes to decide to push a box. Remember the pattern perceive, plan, act: it comes back at the end of the lesson.

diapos.texte: Machines will be capable, within twenty years, of doing any work a man can do.
diapos.notes: The promises of the time were excessive. Twenty years later, in 1985, the field was very far from them. Ask students to find a current promise about AI and to consider how it will be judged in twenty years.

points: 1969: Minsky and Papert show the limits of the single-layer perceptron
1973: the Lighthill report, in the United Kingdom, finds the results disappointing
Computations explode as soon as problems grow
Public funding is cut: this is the “winter”
diapos.notes: An AI winter is a period when disappointment drives away funding and researchers. The curve shows both winters: 1974–1980 and 1987–1993. A point of method: judge a technique on its results, not on its promises.

diapos.texte: AI comes back by turning experts' knowledge into rules. It enters companies, then falls back.
diapos.notes: Fourth stage: the triumph of symbolic AI, the AI of chapter 3 and its tutorial (TD) on forward chaining.

points: A fact base, a base of IF … THEN … rules, an inference engine
1970s: MYCIN, at Stanford, diagnoses blood infections
1980: XCON configures computers for the company DEC
Companies invest: AI becomes an industry
diapos.notes: Link this to session 6: the role play on poetic forms is a small expert system. MYCIN had about 600 rules written with doctors.

points: 1982: Japan launches the Fifth Generation Computer project
1986: Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams popularize backpropagation
Networks with several layers can finally be trained
But computers and data are still lacking
diapos.notes: Backpropagation calculates how to correct each weight of a network from the final error. It is the gradient descent of chapter 3, applied to millions of weights. The idea was ready twenty-five years before its triumph.

points: 1987: the market for specialized Lisp machines collapses
Expert systems are expensive and fail outside their domain
Each new rule contradicts others: they become unmanageable
The word “AI” falls out of favor: people say “advanced computing” instead
diapos.notes: Expert systems are brittle: they know only what has been written into them, and do not know what they do not know. This weakness explains the next turn: learning from data.

diapos.texte: Instead of writing the rules, we give examples. With the Internet, the examples run into the billions.
diapos.notes: Fifth stage: this is the great reversal. It rests on three ingredients: algorithms, data and computing power.

diapos.titre: Two ways to build an AI

points: An expert writes the rules
Explainable: the reasoning can be followed
Brittle outside its domain
Example: an expert system
The machine draws patterns from examples
Often hard to explain
Robust, if there is plenty of data
Example: a spam filter

diapos.notes: Have students classify three objects: a spellchecker, a machine translator, a GPS. Today, the best systems often combine both approaches.

diapos.role: IBM's computer beats the world chess champion
points: Wins 3½ to 2½ over six games, in New York
About 200 million positions evaluated per second
Computing power, not learning: this is still search-based AI
diapos.notes: The event made headlines around the world. But Deep Blue does not understand chess: it calculates moves and evaluates them with rules written by experts. Compare with AlphaGo, which would learn by playing, twenty years later.

evenements.texte: Yann LeCun trains a convolutional network to read postal codes
A program learns backgammon by playing against itself
LeCun's networks read bank checks in the United States
A robot vacuum cleaner enters people's homes
A driverless car wins the DARPA desert race
Watson wins the TV quiz show Jeopardy!; Siri arrives on phones

diapos.notes: Notice that AI becomes invisible: it sorts mail, reads checks, filters spam, without being called AI. This is sometimes called the “AI effect”: as soon as a technique works, people stop considering it intelligence.

diapos.texte: Neural networks with very many layers, trained on huge amounts of data with graphics processors.
diapos.notes: Sixth stage. The word “deep” refers to the number of layers in the network, not to depth of thought.

diapos.titre: A deep network, layer by layer
points: The first layers detect simple features: edges, blobs
The next layers combine them: shapes, textures, parts
The last ones recognize whole objects: “cat”, “car”
Each layer learns by itself what to detect
diapos.notes: Show the animation: the signal crosses the layers from left to right. It is the same with a text: letters, words, phrases, meaning. Nobody writes down what each neuron should detect: it learns it.

diapos.role: An image database that changes everything
points: 2009: ImageNet, over 14 million images labeled by hand
2012: the AlexNet network crushes the image recognition competition
Its error rate falls to 15%, against 26% for the runner-up
diapos.notes: Three ingredients came together in 2012: data (ImageNet), graphics cards to compute fast, and deep networks. It is the start of the current wave. The images were labeled by thousands of workers paid per task: an ethical point to discuss.

points: Defends neural networks through both winters
2018: Turing Award with Yoshua Bengio and Yann LeCun
2024: Nobel Prize in Physics with John Hopfield
diapos.notes: Hinton is an example of a researcher who was right too early: his ideas from the 1980s only really worked in 2012. In 2023, he left Google to warn about the risks of AI.

diapos.titre: Machines also learn language and games

evenements.texte: Words become vectors: “king” − “man” + “woman” ≈ “queen”
Two networks compete to produce realistic images
A DeepMind agent learns 49 video games from the pixels and the score
DeepMind's program beats Lee Sedol at Go, 4 games to 1

diapos.notes: Go was thought to be too complex for computers: it has more possible positions than there are atoms in the universe. AlphaGo combines deep learning and reinforcement learning, the third type of learning in chapter 1.

points: Game two: AlphaGo plays a move no human would have played
Commentators think it is a mistake; it is a winning move
The machine no longer imitates humans: it finds its own strategies
diapos.notes: “Move 37” has become the symbol of machine creativity. Go back to Lovelace's objection: did AlphaGo “create” something? In 2024, Demis Hassabis and John Jumper received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for AlphaFold, which predicts the shape of proteins.

diapos.texte: A new architecture learns to read whole texts. Machines start to write, draw and translate.
diapos.notes: Seventh stage: the one that leads to the chatbots your students already use.

points: Eight Google researchers propose the Transformer
The attention mechanism links each word to all the others
In “The student opened the book because she…”, “she” looks at “student”
All of today's large language models descend from it
diapos.notes: The paper's title has become famous. The animation shows the attention links: thickness indicates importance. The Transformer reads all the words at once, which makes it possible to train huge models.

evenements.texte: Google: a model that understands a word's context
OpenAI: text so fluent that the company hesitates to release it
175 billion parameters; AlphaFold 2 solves the shape of proteins
An image drawn from a sentence
November 30: generative AI reaches the general public

diapos.notes: In five years, we go from a laboratory tool to a service used by hundreds of millions of people. Ask who in the class has already used a chatbot, and for what.

points: A computer only knows numbers
The text is cut into pieces: **tokens**
Each token gets a number, then a long list of numbers: a **vector**
The model never sees letters, only these numbers
diapos.notes: The numbers in the picture are made up for the example. A real vocabulary has tens of thousands of tokens (just over 50,000 for GPT-2); a common word stays whole, a rare or long word is cut into several pieces. The colored columns stand for the vectors: hundreds of numbers per token, learned during training. Refer to the chapter 1 lesson “How an AI ‘understands’ a text”.

points: Each vector is an address on a huge map of meanings
Words with the same neighbors end up close: “cat”, “dog”
The model learns this by itself, guessing hidden words in billions of sentences
The map keeps relations: from “man” to “woman” as from “king” to “queen”
diapos.notes: A game to play with the class: “The ___ drinks milk and sleeps on the sofa.” Everyone guesses “cat” thanks to the neighbors: that is what the model does, on a huge scale. The linguist J. R. Firth put it this way in 1957: “You shall know a word by the company it keeps”. Real maps have hundreds of dimensions; here they are projected onto two. These maps also reproduce the stereotypes of their training texts.

points: The same word can have several meanings: “mouse”
**Attention** links each word to its neighbors
With “cheese”, the mouse is the animal; with “click”, it is the device
The word's vector is recalculated from its context
diapos.notes: This is what sets Transformers (2017) apart from older methods, which gave each word a single vector whatever its meaning. Other examples: “bank” (of a river, for money), “bat” (the animal, the stick). Ask the students for an example in another language: in Arabic, “عين” (the eye, a spring).

points: It splits the text into pieces, the tokens
It calculates the probability of each possible next token
It picks one, adds it to the text, and starts again
Humans then rate its answers to refine it
diapos.notes: It is the bigram model of notebook 08, on an immensely larger scale. Tuning by humans is called RLHF: reinforcement learning from human feedback. Stress this: the model predicts plausible text, not true text.

diapos.titre: A dialogue with a language model
diapos.legende: Fictional example, written for the class

echanges.texte: Explain forward chaining to a literature student.
Imagine a detective: he starts from the clues he knows and applies his rules one by one, until he finds the culprit.
Give me a reference so I can cite this in my thesis.
Careful: always check a reference in a library. I can make mistakes or invent references.

diapos.notes: Compare with ELIZA: this time, the answer is relevant, rephrased and adapted to its audience. But the risk remains: a model can invent a reference, a quotation, a date. This is the subject of the “reference test” activity in the guide.

diapos.texte: The language model no longer just answers: it plans, uses tools and acts.
diapos.notes: Final stage: this is what is in the news. Recall Shakey (1966): perceive, plan, act. The idea of an agent is old; what has changed is that a language model now serves as its “brain”.

points: An agent perceives its environment and acts on it to reach a goal
A thermostat is a very simple agent: it measures, then heats or not
Russell and Norvig (1995) define all of AI as the study of agents
A modern AI agent receives a goal, not just a question
diapos.notes: A definition for students to write down. The difference from a classic chatbot: we no longer ask it to “answer”, we ask it to “do”. Example: “Find three articles on Kateb Yacine, read them and write me a summary sheet.”

points: Goal: what the user asks for
Think: the model plans the next step
Act: it uses a tool (search, calculation, file, browser)
Observe: it reads the result, then starts again until the goal is reached
diapos.notes: Have students follow the animated loop. Each round can succeed or fail; the agent corrects its plan. That is why the tools it can access must be limited and its important actions checked.

evenements.texte: Researchers make a single model alternate between reasoning and actions
GPT-4; models learn to call tools and programs
Models that think before answering; a model operates a computer; the MCP protocol for connecting tools
Agents that browse the Web, write and fix programs
Agents settle into office, research and teaching software

diapos.notes: The 2025 and 2026 entries describe general trends rather than specific products, which change quickly. Invite students to find a recent example and present it in two minutes.

points: Answers a question
Produces text
A single turn
The human does the rest
Pursues a goal
Uses tools and acts
Several steps; it corrects its plan
The human supervises and approves

diapos.notes: The boundary keeps shifting: many chatbots can already search the Web. Remember the criterion: an agent chains actions in the world to reach a goal.

points: Hallucinations: an agent may act on false information
Irreversible actions: deleting, sending, paying; they must be approved
Instructions hidden in a Web page can hijack an agent
Personal data: Algerian Law 18-07 applies
2024: the European Union adopts the AI Act
diapos.notes: A simple rule for students: stay in control of every important action, check sources, and declare AI use in your work. Refer them to the AI use charter in the guide.

points: 2021: the National Higher School of Artificial Intelligence (ENSIA) opens
Arabic, Darja and Tamazight remain less well served by models
Local corpora, built in the humanities and social sciences, are a real contribution
Your theses can contribute: texts, surveys, interviews
diapos.notes: A local anchor point. Languages that are less present on the Web are handled less well by models: it is a question of data, and therefore also of the humanities. Encourage students to imagine a corpus they could build.

diapos.texte: Eight centuries of dreams, seventy years of science, a few years of agents.
diapos.notes: Final part: recap, watch the videos, check what has been understood.

evenements.texte: The first program, for a machine never completed
Can machines think?
AI gets its name
The first AI winter
A computer beats the chess champion
Deep learning wins out
Attention at the heart of language models
Generative AI for everyone; then come the agents

diapos.notes: Have students recite the timeline backwards, from 2022 to 1843. These eight dates are enough to tell the whole story in the exam.

diapos.titre: The families of AI, on a single slide

points: Symbolic: written rules
Machine learning: examples
Deep learning: networks with many layers
Reinforcement: trials and rewards
Weak (narrow) AI: one specific task
Strong (general) AI: every task, hypothetical
Today's agents are still weak AI
… but increasingly versatile

diapos.notes: This table links the lesson to chapter 1 of the course (weak and strong AI, types of learning) and to chapter 3 (types of AI). A modern agent combines several families: a deep model, safety rules, sometimes reinforcement.

diapos.titre: Video: the complete history of AI (1950–2026)
diapos.legende: “The Complete History of AI (1950–2026) - The Rise of Artificial Intelligence”, a documentary in English, on YouTube
diapos.notes: Show a passage chosen in advance rather than the whole video. Ask students to spot three dates from the timeline in the video. The video requires an Internet connection.

diapos.titre: Video: a hundred years of artificial intelligence
diapos.legende: “The Entire History of Artificial Intelligence (Last 100 Years)”, a documentary in English, on YouTube
diapos.notes: For English groups, have students summarize the video orally in English: it is also a language exercise. For the others, use automatic subtitles in the chosen language.

diapos.question: In what year did the term “artificial intelligence” take hold, with the Dartmouth workshop?
diapos.explication: The term appears in the 1955 proposal and took hold with the workshop in the summer of 1956.
diapos.notes: Have the class vote before revealing the answer (R key or button).

diapos.question: Why do we speak of AI “winters”?
choix: Disappointment made funding and interest fall
diapos.explication: After excessive promises, the results were disappointing: funding was cut (1974–1980, then 1987–1993).
diapos.notes: Ask for an example of an excessive promise seen in the lesson: Herbert Simon's quotation (1965).

diapos.question: What distinguishes an agent from a simple chatbot?
choix: It pursues a goal by acting with tools
diapos.explication: An agent chains actions (searching, calculating, writing a file…) and observes the results to reach a goal.
diapos.notes: Go back to the loop: goal, think, act, observe.

diapos.question: Did ELIZA (1966) understand what was said to it?
choix: No: it transformed sentences with rules
diapos.explication: ELIZA spotted keywords and sent back stock sentences. Believing that it understood is the “ELIZA effect”.
diapos.notes: A transition question to the debate: and do today's models understand?

points: The dream is old; AI as a science was born between 1950 and 1956
Two paths alternate: writing the rules or learning from data
The winters remind us to judge by results, not by promises
An agent perceives, plans and acts: from Shakey (1966) to the agents of 2025
Check, stay in control, declare your use: the three golden rules
diapos.texte: Homework: choose a date from the timeline and write ten lines on what it changed, citing a verified source.
diapos.notes: End with the opening question: can a machine think? Collect three reasoned answers. The homework prepares the round table on the origins of AI.
